label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Nana,

Tomorrow is moving day. If Denise has done what she promised, you’re reading this in the kitchen on Kathleen Street on your last night in the house, and I wish more than anything that I were sitting there with you.

I tried to find someone to trade on-call shifts with, but it didn’t work out. Everyone keeps telling me it’s fine, and I know you’ll understand, but I still hate that I won’t be there tomorrow. I didn’t want missing the move to turn into missing the chance to say any of this, so now Denise has to sit there and read me going on at great length. I’m sorry to both of you, but mostly to Denise.

I’ve been thinking about the house all week. Fifty-one years is a long time to live anywhere. You raised half the family in that kitchen, and a good portion of the rest of us were fed, taught, scolded, welcomed, or sent back out to dry more dishes there. Grandpa Walt is part of all those memories too. I know tomorrow isn’t just a matter of putting things in boxes and driving somewhere else.

But I don’t want to talk about the house as though we’re holding a funeral for it. You’re moving, not disappearing, and neither are the things you gave us there. I’ve been remembering so many ordinary moments that didn’t seem especially important at the time. Now I can picture them more clearly than almost anything else from when I was little.

Summers at your house, for instance. You let me stay up to watch the Expos or the Jays on that little TV in the kitchen, provided I dried the dishes. At the time I thought I was getting away with something. Now I understand that you had simply discovered the correct price for baseball. I’m still not sure which of us got the better deal, but I remember sitting there long after I should have been asleep, watching that tiny screen while the rest of the house got quiet. It felt like a very special arrangement between the two of us.

Then there was crib. You taught me when I was about seven, and you never once let me win. Not once. There are childcare experts who might have opinions about this, but I think they should mind their own business. You taught me the rules, you counted honestly, and then you beat me for years. The first time I finally skunked you, when I was fifteen, you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. It remains one of the proudest moments of my life, and also the standard by which I believe all major sporting achievements should be celebrated.

I can still see you on the back steps at six in the morning with your tea. I’d come out and sit with you, and you wouldn’t talk until the cup was finished. Not a word. You weren’t being unfriendly. The tea simply came first, and the rest of the world could wait. I didn’t always have your patience, but I loved those mornings. You taught me that sitting quietly with somebody can be its own kind of conversation. I probably didn’t say that at seven, mostly because I wasn’t allowed to speak, but I noticed.

Even after I grew up and moved to Toronto, you kept finding ways to look after me. When I got the job here, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said, “for pizza, you look thin on the computer.” I have thought about that sentence so many times since. I don’t know exactly how I managed to look thin on the computer, but you saw what you needed to see, and the problem was clearly pizza-related. I still have the card. I used the twenty exactly as instructed, although I don’t think one pizza fully addressed your concerns.

And then last Christmas, when my pager went off during dinner, you asked if the internet was broken again and whether I had fixed it. Honestly, it was one of the better explanations anyone has ever given of my job. Something breaks, they call me, and I try to fix it. I love that you ask me now, “Did anything break?” Usually something has, Nana. Sometimes several things. You’ve just managed to make it sound like a perfectly normal family subject instead of a work conversation.

All of this is why the house matters so much to me. Not just because it’s been there for fifty-one years, and not just because I can walk through it in my head. It matters because you made so many people feel at home there. The house is kind of you, if that makes sense. But then I think some of the house must be in me too: the crib, the staying up a little too late for baseball, the tea before conversation, and the belief that a proper response to good news is to feed somebody.

I also want to tell you how proud I am of you for making this move yourself. You picked Elmwood Terrace. Nobody made you do it. At eighty-eight, you looked at what you wanted next and made your own decision. I know there’s probably sadness mixed in with it, because how could there not be, but I love that you’re excited too. You should be. This isn’t you giving something up. It’s you choosing what comes next, just as you’ve made your own decisions all along.

And Elmwood actually looks nice. Your room is on the second floor, overlooking the parking lot and that big maple. A parking lot may not be the most inspiring view ever devised, but a big maple is a very good start. You can have your tea, look at the tree, and quietly judge everyone’s parking. That should keep you busy until somebody arrives for crib.

They have a crib league there too, which I suspect nobody has properly warned the other residents about. They may think they’re joining a friendly recreational activity. They do not know that you’ve spent Tuesdays sharpening your game against the church ladies. Try to let them settle in before you skunk the entire second floor. Or don’t. You’ve never gone easy on me, so I don’t see why they should receive special treatment.

Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and I’ve asked for the crib board. I think that’s a fair distribution of the family treasures, although I may be biased because I know exactly what I want to do with mine. I hope all the pegs are still with it. If one is missing, I have a suspicious feeling you’ve had a secret supply somewhere and were using it to explain some of those scores.

Thank you for all of it, Nana. For the dishes and baseball, for the quiet mornings, for never letting me win, for the butter tarts when I finally earned them, for the twenty-dollar pizza emergency fund, and for always finding a way to ask about my life even when you were talking about the internet being broken. I hope you know how much of you I carry around with me.

Tonight, have your last cup of tea in that kitchen if you want to. Let yourself feel whatever you feel. Just don’t think of it as the last of everything. It’s the last cup there. The next one will be at Elmwood, with the maple outside your window, and I’ll be sitting with you before too long.

I’m coming up the weekend of December 5, as soon as this rotation is finished. I’ll bring the crib board, and we’ll have the first proper game at your new place. You can show me your room, introduce me to whichever poor souls you’ve already beaten in the crib league, and we can start making some new memories in the spot you chose.

And Nana, after thirty-four years of waiting, I’m not letting you win either.

I love you. I’ll see you December 5. Keep a seat for me, and if you happen to feel like making butter tarts, I wouldn’t want to interfere with tradition.

All my love,  
[Your name]
